extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literature; critics; playwrights
extracted.subtask_description: Literary-criticism guidance on what makes good drama, comedy, tragedy, and character depiction — discussing principles such as universality, unity, naturalness, theatricality, and moral effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depicting the gentlemanly character
rubrics_metrics.description: The gentlemanly character arises out of the feeling of Equality acting, as a Habit, yet flexible to the varieties of Rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the gentleman by his habitual deportment: in both trivial and important details of manners he shows respect to others in such a way that implies an habitual and assured anticipation of reciprocal respect. The trait is conveyed through consistent small acts of demeanour rather than through declared moral excellence or ornamental graces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters as natural growths of human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualities portrayed, even when ludicrous, should be the natural growth of the human mind and such as can be applied to one's own heart or to classes of fellow creatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid caricature divorced from human truth; make comic or satiric traits arise plausibly from human psychology so laughter is mixed with insight rather than contempt. Example praised: Shakespeare and Molière, whose ludicrous traits are nevertheless natural and instructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involution of the universal in the individual
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet must effect an 'involution of the universal in the individual' — to embody universal truth within particular individual form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic excellence requires that general truths be incarnated in specific characters and situations rather than stated abstractly. The universal should be present but clothed in distinctive individual detail (Aristotelian principle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity, fitness, and harmony of parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Both comedy and tragedy should preserve 'a fitness in the parts, and a harmony in the whole' — consistency of structure forming a coherent work of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange incidents and parts so they fit together harmoniously; even if the 'nature' presented is a false or artificial one, internal consistency and structural harmony are virtues that engage the intellect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevation and intellectual engagement in tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic scenes ought to affect us within the bounds of pleasure and in union with the activity of our understanding and imagination; they should transport the mind to a sense of its possible greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid producing mere stupefying sensations or maudlin pathos; aim to elevate the spectator's thought, suspend petty individual recollections, and implant seeds of nobler thought rather than pandering to lowest sympathies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid seeking only story-novelty or sensational surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: If the audience seeks in tragedy only the curiosity of a new plot (the same gratification as a new novel), they will miss the higher poetic pleasures; the manner, language, situations, and interplay of passions matter more than mere novelty of incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on unfamiliarity of the tale to create dramatic interest; the poet's craft in handling familiar stories (language, situations, poetic manner) is often the source of lasting artistic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story as vehicle for poet's excellence, not the primary end
rubrics_metrics.description: The story or fable should be regarded as the means by which the poet displays his appropriate excellence, not as the principal object in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize how incidents are arranged and presented to show poetic skill. Enduring works often reuse familiar incidents but distinguish themselves by the poet's treatment rather than by raw invention of plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish theatrical effect from permanent dramatic genius
rubrics_metrics.description: A theatrical genius who adapts pictures to 'pit and boxes' for transient stage effect (e.g., Kotzebue) differs from a dramatic poet whose works address mankind and endure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of crafting scenes solely for immediate stage spectacle or local effect; such productions may be brilliant in performance but are likely transitory in value. Aim for universal human relevance beyond momentary theatrical tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy should instruct through particularized class-characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy's instructiveness lies in class-characteristics which, when modified and particularized in each person of the drama, yield individuality and deeper insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make comic types specific and individualized so that they teach about human nature; the more precisely and fully realized the characters, the more satisfying and instructive the laughter (example: Shakespearean fools, Molière's characters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject low devices: topical slang, pantomime, and maudlin pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid making the audience laugh by witticisms of the moment, accidents of jig, slang phrases, or clothing common-place morals in crude metaphors; likewise avoid pandering with maudlin tears or pathos that represent meanness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of ephemeral or base devices that trade on sensation rather than art. Such means produce only transient amusement or corrupt moral feeling rather than lasting aesthetic or moral effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral sentiment must be demanding and genuine
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern sentimental plays often present only that part of morality which flatters the audience without requiring true sacrifice or Christian virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure moralizing in drama is not simply flattering or self-congratulatory; authentic moral sentiment should require real sacrifice or serious ethical engagement, not mere comfortable consolations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural restraint over profuse incident-invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Great works (Don Quixote, Ariosto) often show that abundance of incident is not necessary; the artist may purposefully limit invention in service of form and sustained excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake a multitude of incidents for dramatic greatness. Controlled invention and masterly arrangement of incidents can produce deeper and more lasting effect than sheer variety or novelty.
